draft.title: Embedding evidence
card: Embedding means fitting a short quotation into your own sentence, so the quotation and your words read as one flow.
a quotation stands alone as its own sentence, with no link to your point. It reads as a break in your writing.
the quotation completes your sentence and keeps its grammar. Example: Mia feels trapped, as the narrator calls the town "a locked box".
Keep quotations short, often a few words. Quote only the words that carry your point, and use your own words for the rest.
draft.remember: Let your own sentence carry a short quotation, and quote only the words you need.

a.q: Which sentence embeds the evidence best? (The text is an invented story.)
opts: Jon seems lonely, as the narrator calls the house "empty" and "silent"
Jon seems lonely. "The house was empty and silent, and he sat alone"
Jon seems lonely. Here is a quote: "The house was empty"
Jon seems lonely, as the narrator says the house was empty
a.why: The first option fits two short quoted words into the student's own sentence, and the grammar flows. The second drops a long quote in on its own. The last option has no quotation, so it gives no evidence from the words of the text.
a.clue: Look for short quoted words that finish the writer's own sentence.

b.q: A student writes: Lena is brave. "She stepped out into the storm without a coat, a map or any plan at all." What is the main problem with this evidence?
opts: The long quote is dropped in, not woven into a sentence
The quote is too short to show anything about Lena
The word brave should not be used in the first sentence
The quote comes after the student's own point
b.why: The quotation is long and stands alone, so it is dropped in rather than embedded. Placing a quote after your point is normal. The problem is how the quote is joined to the point, not where it sits.
b.clue: Check whether the quote is joined to the student's sentence.
